summary: Standardizes identifiers for HMAC-SHA algorithms used with the DNS TSIG resource record. Previously only HMAC-MD5 and GSS identifiers had been specified. It was standards-track and has been replaced by RFC 8945.

eli5.summary: DNS servers can sign messages to show they are real. This gives names to the extra signature recipes.

questions: how to use hmac-sha256 for tsig
subtitle: Add identifiers for stronger hash algorithms in DNS TSIG.

tldr.problem: DNS TSIG (Transaction Signatures) originally only supported HMAC-MD5, but MD5 is cryptographically weak. Stronger SHA algorithms are needed but had no standard identifiers.
tldr.mechanism: Define standard identifiers for HMAC-SHA-1, HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384, and HMAC-SHA-512 used with TSIG. Also standardize how to truncate HMAC output when shorter MACs are acceptable, and set minimum truncation lengths to prevent excessive weakening.
tldr.outcome: DNS servers can now negotiate and use stronger authentication codes for TSIG. RFC 8945 later updates the mandatory algorithm requirements.

today: HMAC-SHA algorithms are now standard for DNS TSIG. RFC 8945 updates the mandatory algorithm requirements, requiring SHA-256 in addition to MD5 for backward compatibility. MD5-based TSIG should be phased out in favor of stronger algorithms.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
TSIG (Transaction Signatures) [RFC 2845] allows a DNS resolver and server to authenticate each other using a shared secret and a keyed hash. Originally, TSIG only specified HMAC-MD5.SIG-ALG.REG.INT, the identifier for HMAC [RFC 2104] with MD5 [RFC 1321].

MD5 is a 128-bit hash that has known cryptanalytic weaknesses. Attackers have successfully computed MD5 collisions, and the algorithm is considered deprecated for new applications. Stronger alternatives exist: SHA-1 (160 bits), SHA-256 (256 bits), and the larger SHA family (SHA-384, SHA-512).

IANA has also registered gss-tsig for TSIG where the cryptographic operations are delegated to the Generic Security Service (GSS) [RFC 3645].

This RFC standardizes identifiers and implementation requirements for HMAC-SHA algorithms with TSIG, and clarifies how to truncate HMAC output (sending a shorter MAC when the full hash is not needed).
sections.eli5: The recipe for signing DNS messages was weak. This RFC says which new, stronger recipes to use and how to label them officially.

sections.title: Algorithms and Identifiers
sections.content:
TSIG requires prior agreement between resolver and server on the algorithm and key to use. This RFC specifies the following algorithm identifiers (some mandatory, some optional):

Mandatory to implement:

HMAC-MD5.SIG-ALG.REG.INT (the original, for backward compatibility)

hmac-sha1 (HMAC with SHA-1, a 160-bit hash)

hmac-sha256 (HMAC with SHA-256, a 256-bit hash)

Optional to implement:

gss-tsig (GSS-based TSIG)

hmac-sha224, hmac-sha384, hmac-sha512 (other SHA variants)

As an implementation guideline, HMAC-SHA-1 truncated to 96 bits (12 octets) should be implemented to match the truncation used in IPsec and TLS.

By moving to SHA-1, SHA-256, and beyond, DNS operators can resist known attacks on MD5. A longer hash output naturally provides stronger authentication since an attacker must brute-force more bits to forge a valid MAC.
sections.eli5: These are the official names for the recipes: 'hmac-sha1', 'hmac-sha256', etc. Two recipes are required (MD5 for old compatibility and SHA-1 for new systems), and the others are up to the implementer.

sections.title: Truncation and MAC Size
sections.content:
The TSIG RR includes a 'MAC size' field that specifies how many octets of the HMAC output are actually used. RFC 2845 did not define what happens if this size differs from the full hash output length.

This RFC clarifies the three cases:

Case 1: MAC size equals full HMAC output length. Use the entire hash, as originally specified. For example, HMAC-SHA-256 produces 32 octets; use all 32.

Case 2: MAC size is less, but not too much. Truncate the HMAC output (discard trailing octets, keep the initial octets). On receipt, the receiver computes the full HMAC locally, truncates it the same way, and compares. Truncation is allowed as long as the MAC size is greater than the larger of 10 octets and half the hash length. For example, HMAC-SHA-256 (32 octets) can be truncated to 17 octets (half is 16, plus 1).

Case 3: MAC size is much smaller. This is an error. If received, the packet must be dropped and a FORMERR (malformed DNS message) response sent. This prevents truncation to excessively small values that would weaken the authentication to near-useless levels.

The minimum MAC size is therefore the larger of 10 octets and half the hash length. For MD5 (128 bits = 16 octets), the minimum is 10 octets (since 10 > 8). For SHA-256 (256 bits = 32 octets), the minimum is 16 octets (since 16 > 10).
sections.eli5: A HMAC is normally the full hash output (like 32 bytes for SHA-256). But sometimes you can use just the first 16 bytes to save space, as long as you don't cut it down too far or it gets too weak.

sections.title: TSIG Policy and Error Handling
sections.content:
TSIG use is by mutual agreement. Each side typically binds its keys to particular algorithms, so an unknown or unsupported algorithm results in a BADKEY error.

Local security policies may reject a TSIG even if the algorithm is mandatory to implement, if the policy requires a stronger variant. Policies may enforce minimum MAC lengths to ensure authentication is not weakened below an acceptable threshold.

When receiving a TSIG with valid truncation but a MAC that is shorter than the local policy allows, the server returns a new RCODE: BADTRUNC (22). This tells the client that the MAC is too short for the policy in effect.

Implementations that support multiple algorithms and truncations should rank them by presumed strength and accept a stronger algorithm/truncation than the minimum required by policy.
sections.eli5: Each resolver and server decide what recipes they trust. If they disagree, the server can say 'your signature is too short' or 'I don't know that recipe'.
